thread_title: S. leucophylla var. alba Washington Co, AL
breadcrumb: S. leucophylla var. alba Washington Co, AL

posts.body_html:
The first of the fall traps on S. l. var. alba Washington Co AL "Solid White" are about to open. Like many of its fellow Washingtonians this clone produces a steady series of good pitchers spring through summer, takes a small breath, then pumps out big fat fall traps around now. This is in marked contrast to many other leucos which have three distinct phases: spring pitchers, phyllodia (often with summer pitchers mixed in), and fall pitchers. None of my WA Co. plants produces significant phyllodia (hallelujah!), a trait that we think comes from alata/rubra introgression. These are about to pop, so will have more pics in a week or two.
Untitled by Calen Hall, on Flickr
Here is a summer pitcher that's a couple weeks old - nothin' to sneeze at!
Untitled by Calen Hall, on Flickr

posts.body_html:
Beautiful photos Calen!

I wonder if the slow growth of some of these Washington Co. clones (reported in posts a few years ago) is due to a combination of the lack of phyllodia you noted combined with overall low chlorophyll levels in the plant due to the large white areas.  So breeding plants with larger white areas without a phyllodia phase would necessarily create less vigorous/slower growing plants?

I also wonder if anyone trying to breed an all-pink version of the albas by crossing with some of the pink leucos?

A lot of the "old" European albas do seem to both be slow and to represent Washington Co. genetics. The genetics reported on in this thread however are actually very vigorous - at least the clones I have obtained from Mike, not all of which are in this thread. I'm sure he has some slow-growing stinkers as well that just haven't offered any sideshoots to distribute, lol. Not sure why the difference, but it could be that growers in Europe working with a very limited sample of original material did a lot of selfing to concentrate the recessive alba genes and that resulted in inbreeding depression. It is true that these plants have less photosynthetic surface area to work with, but at least the plants in this thread seem to do just fine (they do produce a few very small phyllodes as well). 

Regarding the pink x alba cross: that is a terrible, terrible idea and I don't know why anyone would want to do such a thing!!! JK I think you could get some absolutely spectacular plants that way and I made a few such crosses this year! A solid white, pink blushed clone would be an absolute dream.
